Level 1: The Text-Book Stickler (Strictly Chapter 1)
Standard: Direct recall from the "Historical Background" chapter text. No outside info.
The Company Rule (1773–1858)

1. The Britishers originally came to India in 1608 as traders in the form of the East India Company. In which year did they obtain the 'diwani' (rights over revenue and civil justice) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa? a) 1600 b) 1757 c) 1764 d) 1765

2. Which Act is described as the "first step taken by the British Government to control and regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India"? a) Charter Act of 1813 b) Regulating Act of 1773 c) Pitt’s India Act of 1784 d) Charter Act of 1833

3. Under the Regulating Act of 1773, the Governor of Bengal was designated as the Governor-General of Bengal. How many members were appointed to his Executive Council to assist him? a) Three b) Four c) Five d) Six

4. Which Act provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at Calcutta comprising one chief justice and three other judges? a) Regulating Act of 1773 b) Amending Act of 1781 c) Charter Act of 1793 d) Charter Act of 1853

5. The Amending Act of 1781 (Act of Settlement) exempted which of the following from the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court? a) The Governor-General and his Council for official acts b) The servants of the Company for their official actions c) Revenue matters and collection of revenue d) All of the above

6. Which Act created a new body called the 'Board of Control' to manage political affairs, thus establishing a system of double government? a) Regulating Act of 1773 b) Pitt’s India Act of 1784 c) Charter Act of 1793 d) Charter Act of 1813

7. In 1786, Lord Cornwallis placed two demands to accept the post of Governor-General. One was to be the Commander-in-Chief. What was the second demand? a) To have a council of 10 members. b) To have power to override the decision of his council in special cases. c) To have the power to appoint judges. d) To be independent of the British Parliament.

8. Which Act laid down that the members of the Board of Control and their staff were to be paid out of the Indian revenues? a) Charter Act of 1793 b) Charter Act of 1813 c) Charter Act of 1833 d) Charter Act of 1853

9. The Charter Act of 1813 abolished the trade monopoly of the Company in India EXCEPT for which two specific trades? a) Trade in textiles and spices b) Trade in tea and trade with China c) Trade in opium and indigo d) Trade in salt and trade with Ceylon

10. Which Act authorized the Local Governments in India to impose taxes on persons and punish them for non-payment? a) Charter Act of 1793 b) Charter Act of 1813 c) Charter Act of 1833 d) Charter Act of 1853

11. Which Act made the Governor-General of Bengal the "Governor-General of India" and vested in him all civil and military powers? a) Charter Act of 1813 b) Charter Act of 1833 c) Charter Act of 1853 d) Government of India Act 1858
12. Who was the first Governor-General of India? a) Lord Warren Hastings b) Lord Cornwallis c) Lord William Bentinck d) Lord Canning
13. The Charter Act of 1833 ended the activities of the East India Company as a commercial body. The Company became a purely ______ body. a) Judicial b) Administrative c) Legislative d) Military

14. Which Act for the first time separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s council, creating the Indian Legislative Council? a) Charter Act of 1833 b) Charter Act of 1853 c) Government of India Act 1858 d) Indian Councils Act 1861
15. The Macaulay Committee (the Committee on the Indian Civil Service) was appointed in which year? a) 1833 b) 1853 c) 1854 d) 1858
The Crown Rule (1858–1947)

16. The Government of India Act of 1858 was known as the: a) Act for the Better Government of India b) Act for the Independence of India c) Act for the Federal Structure of India d) Act for the Dominion Status of India
17. Which Act abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors? a) Charter Act of 1853 b) Government of India Act of 1858 c) Indian Councils Act of 1861 d) Indian Councils Act of 1892
18. The Government of India Act of 1858 created a new office, Secretary of State for India. How many members were in the Council of India established to assist him? a) 10 b) 12 c) 15 d) 20

19. Under the Indian Councils Act of 1861, Lord Canning nominated three Indians to his legislative council. Who were they? a) The Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala, and Sir Dinkar Rao b) Dadabhai Naoroji, G.K. Gokhale, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak c) Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Satyendra Sinha, and Tej Bahadur Sapru d) The Nizam of Hyderabad, the Prince of Arcot, and Aga Khan

20. Which Act initiated the process of decentralization by restoring the legislative powers to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies? a) Charter Act of 1833 b) Government of India Act of 1858 c) Indian Councils Act of 1861 d) Indian Councils Act of 1909

21. The Indian Councils Act of 1861 empowered the Viceroy to issue ordinances, without the concurrence of the legislative council, during an emergency. What was the life of such an ordinance? a) 3 months b) 6 months c) 1 year d) Indefinite

22. Which Act gave the legislative councils the power of discussing the budget and addressing questions to the executive? a) Indian Councils Act of 1861 b) Indian Councils Act of 1892 c) Indian Councils Act of 1909 d) Government of India Act of 1919
23. The Indian Councils Act of 1909 is also known as: a) Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms b) Morley-Minto Reforms c) Simon Commission Report d) Cripps Proposals
24. Under the Act of 1909, who became the first Indian to join the Viceroy’s Executive Council as a law member? a) Satyendra Prasad Sinha b) Dadabhai Naoroji c) Sir Dinkar Rao d) C.R. Das

25. "Legalized communalism" is associated with which Act that introduced a system of communal representation for Muslims by accepting the concept of 'separate electorate'? a) Act of 1892 b) Act of 1909 c) Act of 1919 d) Act of 1935

26. Which Act introduced, for the first time, bicameralism and direct elections in the country? a) Indian Councils Act of 1909 b) Government of India Act of 1919 c) Government of India Act of 1935 d) Indian Independence Act of 1947

27. The Government of India Act of 1919 divided the provincial subjects into two parts: transferred and reserved. This dual scheme of governance was known as: a) Federalism b) Dyarchy c) Decentralization d) Autonomy

28. Which Act created a new office of the High Commissioner for India in London and transferred to him some of the functions performed by the Secretary of State? a) Act of 1909 b) Act of 1919 c) Act of 1935 d) Act of 1947

29. The Government of India Act of 1935 provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of provinces and princely states as units. The Act divided the powers between the Centre and units into how many lists? a) Two (Federal and Provincial) b) Three (Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent) c) Four (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent, and Residuary) d) One (Union List)
30. Under the Act of 1935, where were the residuary powers vested? a) Federal Legislature b) Provincial Legislature c) Viceroy d) Secretary of State
31. The Act of 1935 introduced bicameralism in how many out of the 11 provinces? a) 4 b) 6 c) 8 d) 11

32. Separate electorates were extended to the depressed classes (scheduled castes), women, and labour (workers) by which Act? a) Act of 1909 b) Act of 1919 c) Act of 1935 d) Indian Independence Act 1947

33. The Government of India Act of 1935 provided for the establishment of which two specific bodies in addition to the Federal Court? a) Reserve Bank of India and Federal Railway Authority b) Reserve Bank of India and Central Vigilance Commission c) Federal Public Service Commission and Planning Commission d) Reserve Bank of India and Federal Public Service Commission (and Provincial/Joint PSCs)
34. On February 20, 1947, who declared that the British rule in India would end by June 30, 1948? a) Lord Mountbatten b) Clement Atlee c) Winston Churchill d) Ramsay MacDonald

35. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 deprived the British Monarch of his right to veto bills or ask for reservation of certain bills for his approval. This right was reserved for whom? a) The Prime Minister of India b) The Governor-General c) The President of the Constituent Assembly d) The British Cabinet

Level 2 Criteria:
* Standard: Moderate / Conceptual.

* Scope: Focuses on the evolution of laws, connecting different Acts, and testing the "why" and "how" rather than just the "what". It includes standard external knowledge relevant to these Acts (e.g., Poona Pact connection to 1935 Act).
* Total Questions: 30.
Level 2: The Conceptual Bridge (Applied Knowledge)
Company Rule Evolution (1773–1853)

1. The Regulating Act of 1773 is often criticized for creating a chaotic administrative structure. Which of the following provisions of the Act contributed to this specific flaw? a) It made the Governor-General supreme over the Governors of Bombay and Madras in all matters. b) It established a Supreme Court but did not clearly define its jurisdiction vis-à-vis the Supreme Council (Governor-General's council). c) It allowed private trade for Company servants without any restriction. d) It removed the Court of Directors entirely.

2. Which of the following Acts is associated with the "Double Government" system where the commercial and political functions of the Company were separated? a) Regulating Act of 1773 b) Pitt's India Act of 1784 c) Charter Act of 1833 d) Government of India Act of 1858

3. Why is the Charter Act of 1833 considered the final step towards "Centralization" in British India? a) It introduced the portfolio system. b) It deprived the Governors of Bombay and Madras of their legislative powers, vesting them exclusively in the Governor-General of India. c) It established the Federal Court. d) It transferred the power from the Company to the Crown.
4. Consider the following statements regarding the Charter Act of 1853:
1. It separated, for the first time, the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s council.
2. It introduced an open competition system for selection of civil servants.
3. It extended the Company’s rule for an indefinite period, unlike previous Charters. Which of the statements given above are correct? a) 1 and 2 only b) 2 and 3 only c) 1 and 3 only d) 1, 2, and 3

5. The "Mini-Parliament" mentioned in the context of British India refers to: a) The Governor-General's Executive Council under the Act of 1773. b) The Indian Legislative Council established under the Charter Act of 1853. c) The Chamber of Princes established in 1921. d) The Constituent Assembly of 1946.
Crown Rule & Administrative Changes (1858–1909)

6. The Government of India Act of 1858 ended the 'Double Government' system established by Pitt's India Act. What did this specifically entail? a) Abolition of the Board of Control and Court of Directors. b) Abolition of the Governor-General's Council. c) Merger of the Supreme Court and Sadar Adalats. d) Separation of Civil and Military administration.

7. "It was a good government in name, but a bureaucracy in reality." This criticism is often directed at the Act of 1858 because: a) It gave absolute power to the Indians. b) It made the administration responsible to the Indian people. c) The Secretary of State was ultimately responsible to the British Parliament, not the Indian people. d) It removed the Viceroy from the chain of command.
8. The process of 'Decentralization' (restoring legislative powers to provinces) began with the Act of 1861 and was completed by which Act? a) Act of 1892 b) Act of 1909 c) Act of 1919 d) Act of 1935

9. Which Act is credited with initiating the "representative institutions" in India by associating Indians with the law-making process? a) Government of India Act 1858 b) Indian Councils Act 1861 c) Indian Councils Act 1892 d) Indian Councils Act 1909

10. The Indian Councils Act of 1892 increased the functions of legislative councils. Which of the following powers was NOT granted by this Act? a) Power to discuss the budget. b) Power to ask questions to the executive. c) Power to vote on the budget. d) Power to nominate non-official members (indirect election).
Reforms & Dyarchy (1909–1919)

11. The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) are most controversially known for: a) Granting Dominion Status. b) Introducing 'Separate Electorates' for Muslims. c) Establishing the Public Service Commission. d) Introducing Direct Elections.
12. Consider the following statements regarding the Government of India Act, 1919:
1. It relaxed the central control over the provinces by demarcating central and provincial subjects.
2. The provincial budget was separated from the central budget.
3. It introduced 'Dyarchy' at the Centre. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? a) 1 only b) 1 and 2 only c) 2 and 3 only d) 1, 2, and 3

13. In the context of 'Dyarchy' introduced by the Act of 1919 in the provinces, how were 'Transferred Subjects' administered? a) By the Governor with the help of his Executive Council. b) By the Governor with the aid of ministers responsible to the legislative council. c) By the Central Government directly. d) By the Secretary of State.

14. Which of the following acts introduced the principle of "Direct Elections" in India for the first time? a) Indian Councils Act 1892 b) Indian Councils Act 1909 c) Government of India Act 1919 d) Government of India Act 1935

15. The "High Commissioner for India" in London, a post created by the Act of 1919, was meant to: a) Oversee the Viceroy. b) Handle the political functions of the Secretary of State. c) Perform agency functions (procurement, trade) for the Government of India. d) Represent the Princely States in the British Parliament.
Towards Federation & Independence (1927–1947)

16. The Simon Commission (1927) recommendations included which of the following? a) Establishment of a Dyarchy at the Centre. b) Abolition of Dyarchy in the provinces and extension of responsible government. c) Creation of a separate state for Muslims. d) Immediate independence for India.

17. The 'Communal Award' of 1932 led to the 'Poona Pact'. What was the primary outcome of the Poona Pact? a) Separate electorates were granted to the Depressed Classes. b) Joint electorates were retained for Depressed Classes, but with reserved seats. c) The Depressed Classes were removed from the electoral rolls. d) The Hindu Mahasabha rejected the Award.

18. The Government of India Act of 1935 is often described as a "rigid" constitution. Why? a) It could not be amended by the Indian Legislature; the power to amend remained with the British Parliament. b) It did not provide for any fundamental rights. c) It gave veto powers to the Governor-General. d) It was never fully implemented.

19. The 'Instrument of Instructions' in the Act of 1935 guided the Governor-General and Governors in the exercise of their functions. This resembles which part of the current Indian Constitution? a) Fundamental Rights b) Directive Principles of State Policy c) Fundamental Duties d) Preamble

20. Under the Act of 1935, 'Residuary Powers' were given to the Viceroy (Governor-General). In the present Indian Constitution, these powers reside with: a) The President b) The Supreme Court c) The Parliament (Centre) d) The State Legislatures

21. The proposed 'All-India Federation' under the Act of 1935 never came into existence because: a) The Congress Party rejected it. b) The Muslim League rejected it. c) The Princely States did not join it. d) The British Government withdrew the proposal.

22. Which Act explicitly mentioned the "Right of the King to veto bills" or reserve them for his significance, a practice that was effectively discontinued after 1947? a) Act of 1919 b) Act of 1935 c) Indian Independence Act 1947 d) Cabinet Mission Plan
23. Who among the following was the first Indian to be the Governor-General of independent India? a) Dr. Rajendra Prasad b) Pt. Jawaharlal Nehru c) C. Rajagopalachari d) Lord Mountbatten
